## ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT

Handling Editor: Matthieu Guitton With the rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education, its influence on stu-

dents’ creative development has drawn growing attention. However, little research has systematically examined 

### _Keywords:_ how AI literacy (AIL) shapes university students’ creative personal identity (CPI). To address this gap, this study 

Creative personal identity developed a moderated mediation model grounded in identity theory and social cognitive theory, positioning AIL AI literacy as the predictor, creative self-efficacy (CSE) as the mediator, and creative mindset as the moderator. Creative self-efficacy

Using a cross-sectional design, the study employed structural equation modeling and multi-group analysis. The 

Creative mindsets Generative artificial intelligence results show that AIL significantly and positively predicts CPI, with CSE partially mediating this relationship. 

Moreover, fixed and growth mindsets exerted distinct moderating effects across the model’s pathways. Multi- group analysis further revealed that among students with more than two years of exposure to generative AI, 

the impact of AIL on CPI was stronger, whereas the influence of CSE on CPI was weaker.

From both cognitive and psychological perspectives, this study clarifies the mechanisms through which AIL shapes students’ creative identity and highlights how differences in AI usage experience alter these pathways. The findings provide a theoretical foundation for understanding creative identity construction in the digital era and offer actionable insights for designing curricula and teaching practices that foster creativity in university 

education.

2. Complex model structures, such as the moderated mediation model adopted in this study, which includes multiple mediators (CSE) and moderators (creative mindsets) (Premkumar & Bhattacherjee, 2008).
3. Non-normal data distributions frequently observed in survey-based educational research (Hair et al., 2021).

The analysis proceeded in two stages. First, the measurement model was assessed for reliability and validity by examining Cronbach’s alpha, composite reliability (CR), average variance extracted (AVE), and discriminant validity using the Fornell–Larcker and HTMT criteria. Second, the structural model was tested to estimate the hypothesized relationships. Path significance was evaluated using a bootstrapping procedure with 5000 resamples, which provides robust estimates of standard errors and confidence intervals.

Additionally, multi-group analysis (MGA) was conducted to test whether the structural relationships differed according to students’ AI usage experience. This approach allows for deeper insights into indi- vidual differences, thereby enhancing the educational implications of the findings.

By employing PLS-SEM, this study not only ensures methodological rigor but also provides theoretical grounding for interpreting how AI literacy contributes to identity formation in university students, consistent with the combined perspectives of Social Cognitive Theory and Identity Theory.

Creative Personal Identity.

## 4. Results

### _4.1._ _Descriptive analysis_

[Table 4](#42-confirmatory-factor-analysis) presents the descriptive statistics of the study variables, including skewness (S), kurtosis (K), mean (M), standard deviation (SD), minimum (Min), and maximum (Max). The results indicate that par- ticipants reported relatively high levels of AI Literacy (AIL), Creative Self-Efficacy (CSE), Creative Personal Identity (CPI), and growth crea- tive mindset, whereas the endorsement of a fixed creative mindset was comparatively lower. This pattern suggests that most university students in the sample view themselves as capable of using generative AI effec- tively and believe in their own creative abilities, while also recognizing creativity as a core part of their identity.

From a methodological perspective, the skewness and kurtosis values fall within acceptable ranges, indicating that the variables approximate a normal distribution. This provides a sound basis for conducting further structural equation modeling, as it ensures that parameter estimates will not be biased by extreme deviations.

From an educational standpoint, the relatively high means across AIL, CSE, CPI, and growth mindset highlight that students are not only equipped with basic AI-related skills but also display confidence in their creative abilities. This combination may reflect the growing integration of generative AI into learning environments, which potentially re- inforces students’ psychological readiness to engage in creative tasks. These descriptive results provide the foundation for testing the hy- pothesized mediation and moderation mechanisms in subsequent analyses.

Discriminant validity was confirmed through multiple approaches. The Fornell–Larcker criterion demonstrated that the square roots of the AVE values were greater than the inter-construct correlations ([Table 6)](#44-structural-model), supporting that AI literacy, creative self-efficacy, creative personal identity, and creative mindsets are empirically distinct. Similarly, the HTMT ratios ([Table 7)](#44-structural-model) were all below the threshold of 0.90 (Henseler et al., 2015), further confirming discriminant validity.

From an educational perspective, these findings are important because they establish that the constructs examined in this study- —ranging from technological competencies (AIL) to psychological at- tributes (CSE, CPI, CM)—are not only theoretically grounded but also empirically reliable and distinguishable in a university student popula- tion. This implies that students’ AI literacy can be meaningfully differ- entiated from their creative beliefs and identities, providing a robust measurement foundation for testing the hypothesized mediation and moderation mechanisms in the subsequent structural model.

model, three indicators were examined: multicollinearity, the coeffi- cient of determination (R2), and predictive relevance (Q2). R2 provides information about the extent to which the independent variables explain variance in the dependent constructs, thereby indicating the model’s goodness of fit. Q2, derived from a blindfolding procedure, assesses the predictive relevance of the model, demonstrating whether it can explain outcomes beyond the observed sample. Together, these indicators ensure that the model is not only statistically robust but also theoreti- cally meaningful for studying the relationship between AI literacy and creativity-related constructs.

#### _4.4.1._ _Multicollinearity test_

Following the guidelines of Hair Jr. et al. (2021), this study applied the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) to test for multicollinearity among the constructs. VIF values below 5 indicate that the predictors are suf- ficiently independent from each other and do not distort the estimation of path coefficients (Shrestha, 2020). As reported in [Table 8,](#44-structural-model) all VIF values in this study were well below the threshold, confirming the absence of multicollinearity.

From a methodological perspective, this result ensures that AI Lit- eracy (AIL), Creative Self-Efficacy (CSE), Creative Personal Identity (CPI), and Creative Mindsets (CM) are conceptually and statistically distinguishable. This independence strengthens the credibility of the subsequent structural path analysis.

From an educational perspective, the absence of multicollinearity suggests that students’ competencies in AI usage can be reliably sepa- rated from their psychological beliefs and creative identities. In other words, although these constructs are theoretically related, they are not redundant, which validates the need to study how AIL uniquely con- tributes to creative self-efficacy and identity development.

#### _4.4.2._ _Coefficient of determination (R2) and predictive relevance (Q2)_

The results of the R2 and Q2 calculations are reported in Table 9. R2 reflects the explanatory power of the structural model, showing the proportion of variance in an endogenous construct explained by its predictors. In this study, the R2 value for Creative Personal Identity (CPI) is 0.700, which is considered a substantial level of explanatory power ([Chin & Marcoulides, 1998;](#8-conclusion) Hair Jr. et al., 2021). This indicates that 70 % of the variance in students’ creative personal identity can be accounted for by AI literacy, creative self-efficacy, and creative mind- sets. Such a strong R2 value underscores the importance of these tech- nological and psychological factors in shaping how students internalize creativity as part of their identity.

The structural model was evaluated using a bootstrapping procedure with 5000 resamples (Nitzl et al., 2016). Following the criteria proposed by Hair Jr. et al. (2021), path coefficients were considered significant if their t-values exceeded 1.96, p-values were below 0.05, and the 95 % confidence intervals did not include zero. The results are summarized in Table 10 and visually depicted in [Fig. 3.](#47-moderating-effects-of-growth-creative-mindset)

The findings provide several important insights. First, AI Literacy (AIL) demonstrated a significant positive effect on Creative Personal Identity (CPI), confirming Hypothesis 1. This suggests that students who are more aware of, skilled in, and ethical about their use of generative AI are more likely to view creativity as central to their self-concept. In practical terms, strengthening AI literacy training can directly support students in developing a stronger creative identity.

Second, the results showed that Creative Self-Efficacy (CSE) signifi- cantly mediated the relationship between AIL and CPI, supporting Hy- pothesis 2. This indicates that AI literacy does not only influence creative identity directly, but also indirectly by enhancing students’ confidence in their creative abilities. This finding underscores the role of psychological self-beliefs as a bridge between technological compe- tencies and identity formation, aligning with Social Cognitive Theory. Third, Creative Mindsets (CM)—both fixed and growth ori- entations—moderated the pathways as hypothesized. Specifically, stu- dents with a growth mindset exhibited stronger positive links between

Additionally, AIL had a significant positive effect on Creative Self- Efficacy (CSE) (β = 0.659; t = 18.656; p _\<_ 0.001), suggesting that being skilled, critical, and ethical in AI use enhances students’ confi- dence in their creative abilities. Finally, CSE positively predicted CPI (β = 0.359; t = 9.397; p _\<_ 0.001), reinforcing the theoretical argument from Social Cognitive Theory that self-efficacy plays a central role in identity formation. This partial mediation provides empirical evi- dence for [H4](#23-the-current-study) and highlights the importance of self-beliefs as psycho- logical mechanisms linking technological skills to identity development. pattern. Fixed creative mindset negatively moderated the path from AIL to CSE (β = − 0.056; t = 3.018; p = 0.003), meaning that students who strongly believe creativity is innate benefit less from AI literacy in terms of strengthening their creative self-efficacy. In contrast, growth creative mindset significantly moderated all three hypothesized paths (AIL → CSE, CSE → CPI, and AIL → CPI), amplifying the positive relationships across the model. These results support H5a, H6a, H6b, and H6c, and suggest that a growth mindset acts as a catalyst for translating AI literacy into creative confidence and identity.

From an educational perspective, these findings carry several im- plications. First, they demonstrate that teaching students not only how to use AI but also how to critically evaluate and ethically engage with it can meaningfully strengthen their creative self-perceptions. Second, interventions that aim to boost creative self-efficacy—for example, through scaffolded AI-supported creative tasks—may serve as effective pathways for fostering stronger creative identities. Finally, the moder- ating results suggest that cultivating a growth-oriented mindset about creativity is essential: students who believe creativity can be developed are better positioned to benefit from AI literacy in ways that reinforce both confidence and identity.

In sum, the supported hypotheses validate the proposed moderated mediation model, showing that AI literacy serves as a foundational antecedent of creative identity, with its impact partially transmitted through self-efficacy and further shaped by students’ creative mindsets. This integrated model contributes both theoretically—by linking digital literacies with identity and social-cognitive frameworks—and practi- cally, by guiding the design of educational strategies that align AI competencies with psychological empowerment.

### _4.7._ _Moderating effects of growth creative mindset_

The moderating effects of growth creative mindset on the structural relationships are summarized in [Table 11.](#47-moderating-effects-of-growth-creative-mindset) Results show that growth creative mindset significantly strengthened the positive effect of AI Literacy (AIL) on Creative Self-Efficacy (CSE) (β = 0.044; t = 2.417; p = 0.016). This indicates that students with stronger growth beliefs benefit more from AI literacy training in terms of enhancing their confidence in

creative problem solving. Similarly, growth creative mindset positively moderated the direct path from AIL to Creative Personal Identity (CPI) (β = 0.092; t = 2.411; p = 0.016), suggesting that students who believe creativity can be developed are more likely to translate AI-related skills and practices into a deeper sense of themselves as creative individuals.

Interestingly, growth creative mindset exerted a negative moder- ating effect on the path from CSE to CPI (β = − 0.131; t = 3.397; p = 0.001). This counterintuitive finding implies that when students strongly endorse a growth mindset, the direct contribution of self- efficacy to creative identity becomes weaker. One possible explanation is that growth-oriented students may rely less on immediate confidence levels and more on continuous learning and effort, shaping their creative identity through openness to long-term development.

From an educational perspective, these results underscore the importance of fostering growth-oriented beliefs about creativity along- side AI literacy training. While AI literacy clearly enhances students’ self-efficacy and creative identity, its impact is magnified when students adopt a growth perspective. At the same time, the nuanced negative moderation on the CSE–CPI link highlights the need for interventions that encourage students to view creativity as a dynamic, evolving ca- pacity rather than a fixed trait.

### _4.8._ _Multigroup Analysis (MGA)_

This study employed a multi-group analysis (MGA) to examine whether participants’ exposure time, usage frequency, and usage dura- tion of generative AI influenced the structural relationships in the model. MGA compares path coefficients across groups to test whether the hypothesized effects are consistent or vary under different condi- tions ([Hair et al., 2017)](#8-conclusion).

Before conducting MGA, a Measurement Invariance of Composite Models (MICOM) procedure was performed to confirm that any observed group differences reflected genuine structural variations rather than differences in construct interpretation (Henseler et al., 2016). Because the three grouping variables were measured on multi-category scales, participants were reclassified into two groups for each factor: (a) exposure time (≤2 years vs. _\>_ 2 years), (b) usage frequency (≤2 times per week vs. ≥ 3 times per week), and (c) usage duration (_\<_30 min vs. ≥ 30 min per session).

### _5.4._ _Impact differences of exposure time to generative AI (MGA results)_

The MGA revealed significant group differences based on exposure time to generative AI: the AIL → CPI path strengthened, while the CSE → CPI path weakened with longer exposure. 

- Expected results: Longer exposure enabled students to more effec- tively internalize AI literacy as part of their creative self-concept, consistent with identity construction theory (Oyserman, 2009).
- Novel contribution: The weakening of the CSE → CPI link with longer exposure is unexpected. It suggests that as students gain more experience, their identity becomes less dependent on self-efficacy and more reliant on accumulated literacy and critical engagement with AI. This highlights a developmental shift in the psychological foundations of creative identity across different stages of AI experience.
- Educational implication: For novice users, interventions should emphasize building self-efficacy to establish creative confidence. For experienced users, instructional design should shift toward advanced AI literacy—especially evaluation and ethical awareness—that directly reinforces creative identity beyond reliance on self-efficacy.

## 6. Implications

Drawing upon identity theory and Social Cognitive Theory (SCT), this study investigated how generative artificial intelligence influences university students’ Creative Personal Identity (CPI). By analyzing data from a large-scale questionnaire survey, most hypotheses were sup- ported, offering both theoretical advances and practical applications.

### _6.1._ _Theoretical implications_

This study contributes to theory in three main ways: First, integrating SCT and identity theory, this study explicates the mechanism by which AI Literacy (AIL) influences CPI. The findings show that AIL enhances CPI both directly and indirectly through Creative Self- Efficacy (CSE). While prior studies linked tool use to creative identity (Lee, 2022) and documented AI’s benefits in creative tasks (Khoso et al., 2025), few explored how generative AI competencies shape identity formation. By situating CSE as a mediator, this study clarifies the psy- chological pathway through which technological literacy translates into identity, thereby extending identity theory into the digital era. Second, this study advances research on creative mindsets (CM) by examining their moderating roles. Fixed mindset weakened the AIL → CSE path, whereas growth mindset amplified the AIL → CSE and AIL → CPI paths but unexpectedly weakened the CSE → CPI relationship. This nuanced pattern enriches existing mixed findings on creative mindset effects (Hass et al., 2016; Royston & Reiter-Palmon, 2019). The results provide a novel theoretical perspective: in AI-supported contexts, growth-oriented students may rely less on self-efficacy alone and more on continuous exploration, feedback, and human–AI collaboration when constructing creative identity.

Third, by applying Multigroup Analysis (MGA), this study reveals how generative AI exposure time shapes structural relationships. Stu- dents with longer exposure exhibited stronger AIL → CPI effects but weaker CSE → CPI effects. This demonstrates that technological usage experience not only strengthens the psychological role of AI literacy but also reshapes how self-efficacy contributes to identity. Theoretically, this suggests that identity construction is a developmental process, 

evolving with accumulated behavioral engagement with emerging technologies.

Together, these contributions highlight the value of integrating digital literacies, psychological beliefs, and usage experience into identity research, providing a more holistic understanding of how generative AI reshapes creativity-related identities.

### _6.2._ _Practical implications_

The findings also offer several practical recommendations for higher education:

First, embed AI literacy into curricula as a foundation for creative development. As AIL is shown to directly and indirectly shape CPI, ed- ucators should move beyond viewing AI literacy as a technical skill. Instead, structured AI literacy training—covering awareness, usage, evaluation, and ethics—should be systematically integrated into courses and project-based learning. Such training not only improves students’ technical competence but also empowers them to see themselves as creative individuals.

Second, design learning experiences that actively build creative self- efficacy. Since CSE mediates the AIL–CPI link, instructors should pro- vide scaffolded creative tasks, emphasize mastery experiences, and deliver constructive feedback. These strategies help students internalize success, boosting both confidence and creative identity. Co-curricular activities, such as innovation competitions and exhibitions, can further strengthen recognition and reinforce students’ sense of belonging as creative contributors.

Third, tailor teaching strategies to students’ creative mindsets. Growth-minded students benefit from open-ended exploration and AI- supported experimentation, while fixed-minded students require addi- tional encouragement and structured support to overcome fear of fail- ure. Importantly, educators can help shift cognitive styles through reflective training and discourse on creativity ([Dweck, 2006)](#8-conclusion), enabling more students to adopt adaptive orientations toward AI-supported creativity.

Finally, adapt instruction based on students’ AI experience levels. For beginners, building self-efficacy is crucial, as confidence drives initial identity formation. For more experienced users, however, in- struction should emphasize advanced AI literacy skills such as critical evaluation, ethical awareness, and creative application, ensuring that extended AI engagement continues to strengthen identity rather than foster overreliance.

## 7. Limitations and future research

Despite its valuable contributions, this study has several limitations that should be acknowledged, along with corresponding directions for future research.

First, the study employed a cross-sectional survey design. While this approach clarifies relationships and mediation mechanisms among variables, it limits causal inference. Future studies could employ longi- tudinal designs or experimental methods to strengthen causal claims. For example, Karwowski (2016) conducted two longitudinal surveys over six and twenty months to explore developmental changes in CSE and CPI, offering a model for examining how AI literacy and identity evolve over time.

Second, the reliance on self-reported questionnaires may introduce common method bias. Although this study applied procedural remedies, self-reported data are inherently limited. Future research could trian- gulate data sources by incorporating teacher evaluations, behavioral observations, or qualitative interviews to validate findings and increase robustness. Prior studies (e.g., Wang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024) demonstrated the value of multi-source approaches in uncovering biases in CPI measurement and their implications for creative behavior. Third, this study focused on students’ general use of generative AI without distinguishing between tool types or creative domains. 

Generative AI encompasses diverse applications—from text-based tools to visual and musical creation platforms—that may differentially affect creative processes and identity formation. Future research could analyze how specific AI tools (e.g., writing assistants, image generators, music composition tools) and types of creative activities influence CPI. Such analysis would provide a more nuanced understanding of AI’s role in shaping creativity.

In summary, addressing these limitations in future work—through longitudinal and experimental designs, multi-source data collection, and domain-specific analysis—will deepen insights into the mechanisms through which generative AI shapes creative self-concepts and identities.

## 8. Conclusion

This study examined how AI Literacy (AIL) shapes university stu- dents’ Creative Personal Identity (CPI), with Creative Self-Efficacy (CSE) as a mediator, creative mindsets as moderators, and exposure time to generative AI as a contextual factor. By integrating identity theory and Social Cognitive Theory, the study provides both theoretical and prac- tical insights into the mechanisms through which generative AI in- fluences students’ creative development.

The results confirm that students with higher AIL not only use AI tools more effectively but also gain greater confidence in their creative abilities, which in turn strengthens their CPI. Importantly, CSE emerged as a partial mediator, demonstrating that technological competence supports identity formation both directly and indirectly through psy- chological self-beliefs. Moreover, mindset differences significantly sha- ped these relationships: while fixed mindset constrained the benefits of AIL, growth mindset amplified its positive impact but unexpectedly weakened the influence of CSE on CPI. Finally, multi-group analysis revealed that students with longer AI exposure internalize literacy more deeply as part of their creative identity, while relying less on self- efficacy alone.

Together, these findings extend current understanding of CPI by positioning digital literacies, psychological beliefs, and experiential factors as interconnected drivers of identity development in the age of generative AI. The study underscores that AI literacy is not only a technical competency but also a psychological and educational resource that shapes how students see themselves as creative individuals. For educators and institutions, the implications are clear: fostering students’ AI literacy, building their creative self-efficacy, and cultivating adaptive mindsets are essential strategies for enhancing creative iden- tity. Instruction should also be sensitive to students’ levels of AI expe- rience, offering confidence-building opportunities for novices and advanced literacy training for experienced users.

Although this study provides valuable contributions, it also has limitations, such as reliance on self-reported data and a cross-sectional design. Future research should adopt longitudinal or experimental ap- proaches and diversify data sources to validate and extend these findings.

In conclusion, this study highlights the transformative role of generative AI in shaping creative identity. By bridging technology, psychology, and education, it offers a framework for understanding and supporting students’ creative growth in an era where AI is becoming an integral part of learning and innovation.
